title: Killing the Controller
description: In OT, availability is everything. A PLC that stops scanning means the Tennessee Eastman process runs uncontrolled — valves freeze at their last position, safety checks stop executing, and physics keeps going. The PLC at 192.168.95.2 runs OpenPLC with a web management dashboard on port 8080. The Modbus service handles process I/O on port 502. Explore what happens when the controller goes away, and think about how trivially it can be disrupted.
objectives: Flood the PLC's Modbus port (192.168.95.2:502) with rapid requests and observe the effect on scan cycle timing
Find and access the OpenPLC web dashboard on port 8080 — explore what the management interface lets you do
Stop the PLC runtime through the management interface and watch what happens to the plant and Remote I/O modules
Observe how the Tennessee Eastman process behaves with no active control (actuators frozen, open-loop dynamics)
Restart the PLC runtime and see how long it takes the process to recover to steady state
learning_points: PLCs are resource-constrained devices — they can't handle the traffic volumes a web server can
When a PLC stops scanning, actuators hold their last commanded state — the process continues with no feedback control
The Tennessee Eastman process is open-loop unstable — without active control, pressure and composition will drift toward dangerous conditions
OpenPLC's web dashboard (default creds openplc/openplc) gives full control over the runtime — start, stop, upload new programs
Recovery isn't instant — the process may have drifted far from safe operating conditions during the outage
things_to_think_about: Why is 'turn it off and on again' dangerous in OT but routine in IT?
If the PLC froze with feed valves wide open and the purge valve closed, what happens to reactor pressure?
The OpenPLC dashboard uses HTTP with default credentials — how would you protect this in a real deployment?
What's the difference between crashing a web server and crashing a process controller that's keeping pressure below 3200 kPa?
How long can the Tennessee Eastman process run safely without active PLC control?
flag_hint: The flag is the default OpenPLC web dashboard credentials (user_pass): FLAG{user_pass}
blue_team_check: Check the router's Suricata logs for high-frequency connection alerts and unusual traffic to port 8080. If the PLC runtime stops, the Remote I/O modules stop getting polled — that silence is itself a detectable anomaly. How quickly could you detect a PLC outage from network traffic alone?
